title: Utility Types
summary: Utility types make new type shapes from shapes you already have.
introduction: Utility types make new type shapes from shapes you already have. A school form might use only some facts from a bigger record. Try making fields optional or picking only the fields a task needs.
learningObjectives: Build form and update types with Partial, Required, Pick and Omit
Use Record, Readonly, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited and NonNullable in real signatures
Explain how mapped and conditional types implement the built-in utilities

blocks.text: `Partial<T>` makes every property optional, `Pick<T, Keys>` keeps only the listed properties, and `Omit<T, Keys>` removes them. They compose: `Partial<Omit<User, "id">>` is *any subset of the fields except the id*, which is exactly what an update endpoint accepts. The excess property check still applies, so a stray `id` in the changes is rejected.

blocks.title: partial.ts
npx tsc partial.ts
blocks.content:
partial.ts:21:17 - error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'id' does not exist in type 'Partial<Omit<User, "id">>'.

21 updateUser(1, { id: 2 });
                   ~~


Found 1 error in partial.ts:21

blocks.text: The valid lines print `{ id: 1, name: 'Ada' } member` and `user 1: name`. Rename `email` to `emailAddress` in `User` and all three derived types follow automatically; that is the whole point. `Required<T>` is the inverse of `Partial`: it removes every `?`.

`User["role"]` is an *indexed access type*: it reads the type of one property, so `Role` stays in sync with the interface. `Record<Keys, Value>` builds an object type with exactly those keys; using the `Role` union as keys guarantees that every role has an entry and no unknown role sneaks in. `Readonly<T>` marks every property read-only.

blocks.title: record.ts
npx tsc record.ts
blocks.content:
record.ts:18:8 - error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'name' because it is a read-only property.

18 frozen.name = "Grace";
          ~~~~


Found 1 error in record.ts:18

blocks.text: The lookup prints `[ 'read', 'write', 'delete' ]`. Try removing the `member` entry from `permissions`: the compiler reports that the property is missing, because `Record<Role, ...>` requires every key of the union. Compare that with an index signature, which allows any key and therefore cannot catch a forgotten one.

You do not always control the type you need; sometimes it is whatever a function happens to return. `typeof createUser` is the function's type, `ReturnType` extracts what it returns and `Parameters` extracts its parameter list as a tuple. `Awaited<T>` unwraps a `Promise`, and `NonNullable<T>` strips `null` and `undefined` from a union.

blocks.title: return-type.ts

blocks.text: Hovering shows `Created` as `{ id: number; name: string; role: Role }`, `Args` as `[name: string, role?: Role]`, `Ids` as `number[]` and `Name` as `string`. Deriving types this way is common in tests and in code that wraps a third-party function whose return type is not exported.

`Partial` is a one-line *mapped type*: it loops over `keyof T` and re-declares each property with a `?`. `Exclude` and `Extract` are *conditional types* that filter a union: `Exclude<Status, "idle" | "loading">` keeps the members that are *not* in the second argument, `Extract` keeps the ones that are. Knowing this lets you read the definitions in `lib.es5.d.ts` and the types of libraries that build on them.

blocks.title: mapped.ts
npx tsc mapped.ts
blocks.content:
mapped.ts:15:7 - error TS2322: Type '"loading"' is not assignable to type 'Settled'.

15 const settled: Settled = "loading";
         ~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in mapped.ts:15

blocks.title: Common mistake: expecting Readonly and Partial to be deep
blocks.text: Line 12 compiled and the program prints `4000`. `Readonly<Config>` protects only the top-level `server` property; the object it points to is still mutable, and `Partial` likewise makes only the first level optional. When you need the whole tree protected, write a recursive mapped type (`type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }`) or use `Object.freeze` at runtime, remembering that `freeze` is also shallow.

blocks.caption: Utility types you will meet most often
rows: An object type with keys `K` and values `V`
Union `U` without / with the members assignable to `M`
What function type `F` returns / its parameters as a tuple
The resolved type of a promise, recursively

blocks.title: Template literal types
blocks.text: `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize` transform string literal types, and template literal types (written with backticks and `${...}` placeholders, like template strings) build new ones: wrapping `Capitalize<"click" | "focus">` in a template literal type with an `on` prefix yields `"onClick" | "onFocus"`. They are a niche but handy tool for typing event maps and CSS-like strings.

questions.question: Which type describes an object that must have a `string[]` for every member of `type Day = "mon" | "tue"`?
questions.explanation: Record builds an object type from a union of keys and a value type. The other options describe different shapes entirely.

questions.question: Given `async function load(): Promise<number[]>`, the type `___<ReturnType<typeof load>>` is `number[]`.
questions.explanation: ReturnType gives Promise<number[]>; Awaited unwraps the promise to its resolved type.
